title: Infinity Nets AB
altText: An abstract etching covered edge to edge with small repeated marks that form a dense, net-like pattern. There is no clear object or figure; the pattern spreads across the whole sheet.

context: Yayoi Kusama is a Japanese artist. The Cleveland Museum of Art describes this 1994 etching, printed by Kihachi Kimura, as part of her Infinity Nets series on infinite repetition and space, in which allover marks blur the line between figure and ground.

descriptions.k: Tiny marks fill the whole picture. They repeat again and again, like a net. There is no one thing to point to. Where do your eyes go? Try to follow the pattern with your finger.
descriptions.g12: Yayoi Kusama is an artist from Japan. In this print, small marks repeat across the whole page like a net. There is no person or animal. Your eyes keep moving. What do you notice when you look closely? Does the pattern ever seem to end?
descriptions.g35: Yayoi Kusama, a Japanese artist, made this etching in 1994. It belongs to her Infinity Nets series, where tiny marks repeat across the whole sheet so it feels like it could go on forever. There is no main object to look at. Look closely: how do the repeated marks work together, and what happens to your eyes as you look?
descriptions.g68: This 1994 etching is part of Kusama's Infinity Nets series about infinite repetition and space. The Cleveland Museum notes that the marks cover the entire surface and blur the line between figure and ground, so no single spot becomes the subject. A printer, Kihachi Kimura, helped produce it. Think about how repeating a simple mark thousands of times can create a pattern, a rhythm, and a feeling of endlessness.
descriptions.g910: In Infinity Nets AB, Kusama uses repetition as both method and subject. According to the Cleveland Museum, the series explores infinite repetition and space, and its allover marks blur figure and ground. With no focal point, the eye keeps moving, which can feel hypnotic or meditative. The etching was printed by Kihachi Kimura in an edition of fifty, showing how a handmade, repetitive mark can be translated into a multiple.
descriptions.g1112: Kusama's Infinity Nets, which she began in the late 1950s and continued through the 1990s per the Cleveland Museum, treat repetition as a way to dissolve the hierarchy between figure and ground. This 1994 etching, printed by Kihachi Kimura in an edition of fifty, translates that practice into print. The allover field resists a focal point and invites open readings: as pattern, as space, or as a record of sustained, repetitive labor. The meaning of such repetition is debated, and viewers are free to weigh more than one.

teacherNote.context: A 1994 etching by Yayoi Kusama from her Infinity Nets series, printed by Kihachi Kimura in an edition of 50, per the Cleveland Museum.
directions: Have students fill a small square with one repeated mark and talk about how their attention changes while drawing.
Ask students to compare a pattern with a focal point (such as a portrait) with an allover pattern and explain how each directs the eye.
Discuss how making many copies from one plate is similar to and different from making a unique painting.
